title: A review of the effects of architectural stimuli on human psychology and physiology
review_question: To identify and categorize elements of building architecture that have been demonstrated through empirical research to affect human physiological and psychological function, focusing on biologically ingrained responses applicable cross-culturally and independent of personal experience.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Limited to physiological and psychological responses framed under sensorimotor and emotion-valuation categories due to their biological foundation and ubiquity. Excluded gustation. Primarily published, peer-reviewed academic papers documenting empirical research. Forward citation searches for highly relevant empirical research. Excluded conflicting research. Summarily covers building design characteristics regulated by codes (thermal, indoor air quality).

Thigmotactic organisms, such as humans, maintain close proximity to the perimeter of a novel space as an instinctive energy-conserving strategy

findings.consequent: Spatial learning (first phase), boundaries definition, spatial map construction, escape routes identification, egocentric frame of reference
findings.quote: This behaviour is sometimes known as wall-following [109], and plays an essential role in the first phase of spatial learning [108]. Sussman and Hollander [110] posit that this behaviour provides a sense of safety and protection afforded by the fact that at least one side of the body is sheltered from potential threats. Additionally, thigmotaxis allows for a systematic identification of potential escape routes from a space and enables the formation of an egocentric frame of reference, both of which contribute to the development of a cognitive map

findings.antecedent: Golden Rectangle (oriented with larger dimension along horizontal axis)
findings.consequent: Efficient scanning by human brain, aesthetic preference, cognitive strain, desirability, productivity, wellbeing
findings.quote: The Golden Rectangle has a length that is 1.618 times its width [102]. It is a rectangle that has existed in architectural history at least as far back as the acient Greeks and was believed to have near mystical powers [102]. The proportions of the Golden Rectangle are such that when one side is split into a square, another Golden Rectangle is created [102]. Therefore, multiple divisions of the Golden Rectangle into squares along successive scales produces a fractal pattern. The presence of the Golden Rectangle is positively correlated with aesthetic preference in architecture [97]. Bejan posits that preference for the Golden Rectangle results from an evolutionary selection based on energy conservation [123]. When scanning an environment, the human brain uses different neurons for different orientations [124]. In other words, some neurons specialize in horizontal scans, others in vertical scans, and others in scans at an angle [124]. The horizontal scan is proportionally more rapid than the vertical scan in the same proportion as the length to height of the Golden Rectangle, i.e., the proportions of the Golden Rectangle allow for the full horizontal and vertical scanning of the stimuli to occur simultaneously [123]. Therefore, the Golden Rectangle has the optimal dimensions for efficient scanning by the human brain, which could explain why it is a desirable shape to people. It should be noted, however, that Bejan's hypothesis is only valid when the Golden Rectangle is oriented with the larger dimension along the horizontal axis. The sizing of façades, interior walls, and other architectural elements of a building according to the dimensions of the Golden Rectangle could reduce cognitive strain, increase aesthetic preference and contribute to the desirability of these spaces or features. This, in turn, might influence occupant productivity and wellbeing.

synthesis_conclusions: The built environment affects human physiology and behaviors through biologically engrained mechanisms.
Architecture can impact human health, happiness, and physiological function, and can be leveraged to produce specific physical and behavioral outcomes.
Light, color, complexity, viewing nature, olfaction, audition, and some forms of geometry have documented psychological and physiological impacts.
Architectural design can be optimized for specific occupancy types to elicit desired responses.
Manipulation of artificial and natural lighting can contribute to occupant health and wellbeing, and elicit specific psychological and physiological responses.
Color can influence consumer behavior and performance, with red potentially inhibiting performance in anxiety contexts and green promoting creativity.
Curvilinear forms can increase preference and feelings of wellness, while open spaces and bilateral symmetry reduce stress and increase pleasurable feelings.
Integration of fractals with dimensional values of 1.3-1.4 can contribute to stress reduction and relaxation.
Natural materials and smooth, graspable dimensions can impart positive physiological responses.
Hospitals can benefit from architecture leveraging these geometries for improved patient outcomes.
evidence_gaps: Many unsubstantiated affirmations in the literature regarding pareidolia, thigmotaxis, object affordance, the Golden Rectangle, and somatosensory stimuli in architecture.
Limited research into the relationship between architecture and the somatosensory, auditory, and olfactory systems.
Need for further research to validate much of the conjecture currently found in the literature.
Need for further research covering a greater diversity of stimuli for olfactory and auditory senses to develop a more holistic understanding.
Need for more field research to reinforce extant empirical data, especially for contentious theories like fractals and colors.
Development of metrics to measure architectural influence on thigmotactic behavior.
heterogeneity_sources: Cultural conditioning vs. universal biological traits (for color research)
Emotional states of subjects (influence aesthetic evaluations)
Context of stimuli (important for preference and interest judgments)
Controlled settings, 2D images, short exposure periods (may invalidate real-world applicability)

moderators.effect: Influences how individuals experience the built environment, e.g., design background affects preference for angular vs. curvilinear spaces.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Research subjects with design background preferred sharp angles, while those without preferred curvilinear spaces.

moderators.effect: Plays a dominant role in how color is perceived and what responses are elicited; influences responses to curvature and angular forms.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Findings from Europe and North America may not be representative of universal biological traits; specific color palettes may be effective only for homogenous cultures or specific demographics.

moderators.effect: Modulates preference for curved objects (only if neutral or positive).
Plays an important role in how the odor is perceived and its effects.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Familiar odors can be difficult to identify out of context.

moderators.effect: May vary the perception of contrast in colors.
Contributes to future perception of color and odor.

limitations: The review primarily covers research conducted in Europe and North America, potentially limiting generalizability to universal biological traits due to cultural conditioning.
Expertise and exposure of subjects can confound documented responses, as they influence aesthetic processing and preferences.
Emotional states of research subjects can influence their aesthetic evaluations, confounding results.
The subjectivity of odor perception and influence of context and beliefs limit the generalizability of olfactory findings.
The majority of research is conducted in controlled settings using representational images or simple stimuli, which may invalidate findings when applied to real-world settings.
The review's focus on single-sense stimuli may not capture cross-modal effects, where multiple senses stimulated simultaneously could yield different experiences.
Some studies involving viewing nature did not isolate for visual stimuli, potentially skewing results due to confounding variables from other senses.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Restorative environments, including certain architectural designs, can restore directed attention and reduce mental fatigue.
Exposure to certain environments, particularly those with natural elements, can lead to physiological and psychological stress reduction.
Humans have an innate tendency to connect with nature and other living systems, influencing preferences for biophilic architectural elements.

mechanism_chain.description: Architectural design incorporating natural light influences human physiology and psychology primarily through its impact on circadian rhythms and subsequent hormonal regulation.
